subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 9 periods = 405 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 45min

periods.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of current
periods.activity_description: A magnetic compass is placed beneath a current-carrying wire in a simple circuit. Students observe the compass needle deflecting when the switch is closed and returning when the switch is opened, establishing that a flowing current produces a magnetic effect that vanishes when current stops.

roles.role_description: Sets up the circuit demonstration, operates the switch, and directs students to observe and record the needle position before, during, and after current flow.
Observe the compass needle, record its position at each stage, and note what changes when the switch is opened or closed.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the opening scenario from the science exhibition — an iron nail wrapped with wire lifting clips — and asks students to predict what a compass near a wire might do when current flows.
Teacher assembles the circuit and guides the class through three conditions: switch open, switch closed, switch reopened; students record compass needle direction for each in a results table.
Students compare their recorded observations and articulate a sentence describing what the current does to the space around the wire.
Teacher introduces the term magnetic field and draws out the key pattern: current on — field present; current off — field gone.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit anchors the entire chapter in a directly observable phenomenon, so let the compass needle surprise students before naming anything. Watch for the common error of attributing the needle deflection to the battery itself rather than to the current in the wire — redirect attention to the wire's position relative to the compass. A useful checkpoint: students are ready to move on when they can state unprompted that the effect disappears when the switch opens.

periods.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of current
periods.activity_description: Students wrap insulated wire around an iron nail and connect it to a cell. They test whether the nail attracts iron paper clips when current flows and whether the clips fall off when current is stopped, directly recording the presence and absence of the magnetic effect.

roles.role_description: Construct the coil-nail assembly, operate the switch, and systematically record which objects are attracted and what happens when the circuit is broken.
Circulates to ensure firm connections, prompts groups to repeat the on-off cycle, and consolidates observations in a shared class table.

time_bands.activity: Brief recall of the previous unit's finding — current produces a magnetic field — and teacher frames the question: can we make a stronger, more useful magnetic effect by winding wire into a coil around iron?
Groups wind wire around nails, connect circuits, test attraction of paper clips in the on state, release them in the off state, and record observations in a results table.
Groups report findings; teacher records a class summary showing that all groups observe attraction with current and no attraction without current.
Teacher introduces the term electromagnet and distinguishes it from a permanent magnet by its on-off controllability.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the previous unit's compass observation by giving students a tangible, controllable magnetic device to construct. A frequent error is loose wire connections producing weak or intermittent attraction — prompt groups to check each junction before concluding the effect is small. Ask groups to predict what would happen if they used more turns before moving to the next unit, planting the question that Stage 2 will investigate.

periods.activity_description: Students form a cylindrical coil on a paper cylinder, place compasses at both ends to identify North and South poles, insert an iron nail to observe the increase in strength, and then reverse the current direction to observe pole reversal — systematically classifying the electromagnet's properties against those of a bar magnet.

roles.role_description: Construct the cylindrical coil, use compasses to identify poles at each end, note the effect of inserting the iron core, and record what happens to the poles when connection leads are swapped.
Poses each investigative question in sequence, prompts groups to record before-and-after results, and facilitates comparison of group findings.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the previous unit's electromagnet construction and poses three investigation questions: Does the coil have poles? Does an iron core change its strength? Does reversing current change the poles?

Groups build the paper-cylinder coil, use compasses at each end to determine North and South poles, insert the nail and recheck strength, then swap battery leads and recheck pole identity — recording results at each step.
Class compares findings across groups and builds a shared list of electromagnet properties: has N and S poles, iron core increases strength, reversed current reverses poles.
Teacher asks students to classify: in what ways is the electromagnet like a bar magnet, and in what ways is it different? Students articulate at least two similarities and one difference.

periods.teacher_notes: In the previous unit students only confirmed that the electromagnet attracts — this unit extends that to the full property set. A common confusion is that inserting the iron core is thought to change the poles rather than only the strength; ask groups to re-check pole identity before and after insertion to separate the two variables. Groups that finish the pole-reversal investigation early can be asked to predict what varying the number of turns would do, anticipating the next unit.

periods.activity_description: Students systematically vary the number of cells and the number of coil turns, counting how many paper clips the electromagnet lifts in each condition. They classify results into a structured table to identify which variables increase magnetic strength and which do not.

roles.role_description: Plan and carry out a fair test — varying one factor at a time — and record the number of clips lifted for each combination in a results table.
Guides groups to keep one variable constant while changing another, probes reasoning with questions such as 'What are you keeping the same?', and consolidates findings.

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the previous unit's property list and frames today's investigation: students must find out whether current strength (number of cells) and coil turns each affect lifting power, and how.
Groups conduct the fair test: first vary cells while keeping turns constant and record clip counts; then vary turns while keeping cells constant and record again.
Groups share data; class identifies the pattern — more cells means more current means stronger magnet; more turns also means stronger magnet.
Teacher consolidates: electromagnet strength depends on current magnitude and number of turns; these are the two controllable variables.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit shifts the same hands-on approach from descriptive observation (previous unit) to systematic fair-test investigation, raising the cognitive demand. Watch for groups that change both variables at once — intervene early with the question 'How do you know which change caused the effect?' to redirect them to fair-test reasoning. Students are ready to move on when they can state both controlling variables and predict the direction of each effect.

periods.stage_label: Observe and explain the heating effect of current
periods.activity_description: A nichrome wire is connected in a circuit. Students touch the wire before current flows and again after the switch is closed, observing that the wire becomes warm. A second trial with two cells allows students to compare heat produced under different current levels, leading them to articulate the heating effect and its dependence on current magnitude.

roles.role_description: Assembles the nichrome-wire circuit, supervises safe wire-touching procedure, and sequences the one-cell and two-cell trials.
Observe and record wire temperature (cool / warm / hot) before and after current flow for each trial, then explain why the wire becomes warm.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the new phenomenon: just as current produces a magnetic effect, it may also produce a thermal effect — students predict what will happen to a wire when current flows through it.

Teacher connects the circuit; students touch the nichrome wire before the switch is closed (record: cool), then after closure with one cell (record: warm), then repeat with two cells (record: hotter) — findings are logged in individual observation sheets.
Students write an explanation: why does the wire get warm? Teacher draws out the idea that the conductor resists current flow and this resistance converts electrical energy to heat.
Teacher introduces the term heating effect of electric current and notes that the amount of heat depends on current, material, thickness, length, and duration.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the second major effect of current and is best positioned as a genuine discovery — let students predict before they observe, so the warmth of the wire is confirmatory rather than demonstrated. A frequent misconception is that the wire heats because electricity itself is 'hot'; redirect to the idea of resistance — the wire opposes current flow, and that opposition releases energy as heat. Confirming students can link more current to more heat before moving on is a useful checkpoint.

periods.stage_label: Observe and explain the heating effect of current
periods.activity_description: Students examine the range of everyday appliances — room heaters, electric kettles, irons, hair dryers, immersion rods — that deliberately exploit the heating effect, and contrast these with situations where the same effect causes problems: energy loss in transmission, overheating, plastic damage, and fire risk. Students categorise each case as intended or unintended use.

roles.role_description: Presents each appliance and each problem scenario systematically, asks students to identify the heating element and its purpose, and draws out the dual-nature conclusion.
Complete a two-column table — intended heating effects versus unintended heating effects — and justify each entry in one sentence.

time_bands.activity: Quick recall: students name the heating effect and its dependence on current, connecting the previous unit's observation to today's application focus.
Teacher systematically presents each appliance category and each problem scenario; students populate the two-column table as each example is discussed.
Students compare tables with a neighbour, reconcile any disagreements, and select one unintended effect they consider most serious — they draft a one-sentence explanation of why it is harmful.
Teacher consolidates: the same physical mechanism (resistance → heat) is harnessed in some devices and causes damage in others; understanding it allows engineers to design for or against it.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established the mechanism; this unit asks students to apply it to familiar and unfamiliar contexts, raising demand from observation to application. A common confusion is treating 'energy loss' during transmission as a separate phenomenon rather than the same heating effect operating where it is not wanted — make this link explicit. The two-column categorisation task doubles as a formative checkpoint: students who can justify each entry understand the dual nature of the effect.
materials: Chalkboard or projected list of appliances

periods.stage_label: Construct and explain sources of electric current
periods.activity_title: Lemon Power — Building a Voltaic Cell
periods.activity_description: Students construct a Voltaic cell using lemons, copper wire, and iron nails, connecting the assembly to a LED. They observe the LED lighting up and connect the observation to the principle that a chemical reaction between two different metals and an electrolyte produces electric current.

roles.role_description: Insert copper and iron electrodes into the lemon, connect them in a circuit with a LED, and record whether the LED lights — then vary the number of lemon cells to observe the effect.
Guides electrode insertion, explains the role of lemon juice as electrolyte, and connects the student-built cell to the historical Voltaic cell described in the chapter.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the question: the chapter's circuits have all used cells — but what is inside a cell that produces current? Students share prior ideas before any explanation is given.
Groups construct lemon cells, test each lemon alone and then connect two in series, recording whether and how brightly the LED lights in each configuration.
Class pool of results: students identify which variables (number of lemons, electrode material) affect the LED brightness and reason about why.

Teacher formalises: electrolyte + two different metals → chemical reaction → electric current; introduces the name Voltaic cell and notes that current flows from positive to negative terminal in the external circuit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit pivots from the effects of current to its source, so brief the class on the shift explicitly — they have been asking 'what does current do?' and now ask 'where does current come from?' A common confusion is that the lemon itself generates electricity; redirect to the interaction between the two different metals and the acid, since neither electrode alone nor the lemon alone suffices. Groups that observe no LED response should first check that their two electrodes are different metals before assuming the lemon is 'dead'.

periods.stage_label: Construct and explain sources of electric current
periods.activity_description: Students examine the internal structure of a dry cell — zinc container as negative terminal, central carbon rod as positive terminal, paste electrolyte — and compare it to the Voltaic cell. They then distinguish single-use dry cells from rechargeable batteries, noting structure, portability, lifespan, and disposal considerations including e-waste.

roles.role_description: Presents a labelled cross-section of the dry cell, guides comparison with the Voltaic cell structure, and introduces the rechargeable battery spectrum from watch batteries to electric-vehicle packs.
Complete a structured comparison table — Voltaic cell, dry cell, rechargeable battery — across five attributes: electrolyte form, portability, reusability, lifespan, and disposal requirement.

time_bands.activity: Recall of the previous unit: students state what the three components of a Voltaic cell are (two electrodes, electrolyte) and how current is produced.
Teacher presents dry-cell structure with labelled diagram; students fill in the Voltaic cell and dry cell columns of the comparison table as each attribute is discussed.
Teacher extends to rechargeable batteries — Li-ion type, charge-discharge cycles, solid-state future technology — students complete the third column of the table and add a note on safe disposal.
Students use their completed table to articulate one advantage and one limitation of each cell type, preparing to reason across all three types in the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit gave students a hands-on encounter with the Voltaic cell; this unit formalises that knowledge and extends it to the devices students encounter daily. A common confusion is treating a rechargeable battery as fundamentally different in principle from a dry cell — both involve electrodes and electrolyte, but the chemistry is reversible in one and not the other. The comparison table is a formative checkpoint: students who can complete it correctly with justifications are ready to reason across both effects and both sources in the closing unit.
materials: Labelled dry-cell cross-section diagram (drawn or projected)

periods.stage_label: Reason across effects and sources: electromagnets, heating, and cells in integrated application
periods.activity_title: From Cell to Effect — Designing an Explanation
periods.activity_description: Students receive a set of unfamiliar application scenarios — an electric bell, a lifting electromagnet in a scrap yard, an electric iron, and a rechargeable-battery-powered device — and must trace the complete chain: what type of cell or battery supplies current, how the current produces the relevant effect (magnetic or heating), and what property of the electromagnet or heating element is being exploited. Students produce a structured written explanation for each scenario.

roles.role_description: Discuss each scenario, identify the relevant effect and source, and collaboratively draft a chain-of-reasoning explanation covering source → current → effect → application.
Circulates to probe reasoning, challenges groups with follow-up questions such as 'What would happen if you reversed the current in the bell's electromagnet?', and facilitates whole-class sharing.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the four scenarios on the board and asks groups to first sort them by which effect (magnetic or heating) they primarily exploit — a quick classification before the deeper explanation task begins.

Groups work through each scenario in turn, writing a chain-of-reasoning explanation: cell/battery type → current produced → effect produced → specific property (e.g. controllable poles, strength variables, resistance-to-heat conversion) → application outcome.
Two groups share contrasting scenarios (one magnetic, one heating); class evaluates whether the chain is complete and accurate and suggests corrections.

Teacher draws the chapter's dual arc together: electricity produces two distinct physical effects — each exploitable and each manageable — and both depend on understanding the source that supplies the current.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit asks students to move across the full chapter arc — from source to effect to application — and is deliberately set in unfamiliar application contexts rather than the chapter's own activities. Watch for groups that describe what a device does without explaining the underlying electrical chain; prompt them with 'what is the current doing inside that component?' to push beyond description toward causal reasoning. The four scenarios are designed so that each group will encounter at least one from each effect domain, ensuring full-chapter coverage in every discussion.
materials: Four scenario cards or board display
Lined paper or structured explanation sheet
homework: Choose one household appliance that uses the heating effect and one that uses the magnetic effect of current. For each, explain in three sentences: what type of cell or power source supplies current, which effect is produced, and what specific property of that effect makes the appliance work.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of current
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe compass needle deflection in a current-carrying wire circuit and construct a simple electromagnet from a coil-wound nail, recording the presence and disappearance of the magnetic effect as the circuit is opened and closed.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe what happens to a compass needle near a current-carrying wire when the circuit is opened and closed, and can construct a basic electromagnet and demonstrate that its magnetic effect is present only when current flows.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students identify the North and South poles of an electromagnet using compasses, observe that inserting an iron core increases strength, demonstrate pole reversal by reversing current, and conduct a fair test to classify how current magnitude and number of turns each affect magnetic strength.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify the poles of an electromagnet, classify how varying current and coil turns affects its strength, and explain that reversing current direction reverses the poles.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and explain the heating effect of current
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe that a nichrome wire becomes warm when current flows and hotter with greater current, explain the mechanism of resistance converting electrical energy to heat, and categorise everyday appliances and problem scenarios as intended or unintended applications of the heating effect.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain that resistance in a conductor converts electrical energy to heat and can categorise examples of the heating effect as intentional (appliances) or unintentional (energy loss, damage), with a one-sentence justification for each.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Construct and explain sources of electric current
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students construct a lemon-based Voltaic cell and connect it to a LED, then compare the Voltaic cell, dry cell, and rechargeable battery across structure, portability, reusability, and disposal requirements in a structured table.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain how a chemical reaction between two different metals and an electrolyte produces electric current, and can compare Voltaic cells, dry cells, and rechargeable batteries across at least four attributes with justification.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Reason across effects and sources: electromagnets, heating, and cells in integrated application
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students trace the complete chain from power source through current to magnetic or heating effect for a set of unfamiliar application scenarios, producing chain-of-reasoning explanations that integrate electromagnet properties, heating effect mechanism, and cell or battery type.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can construct a complete chain-of-reasoning explanation for an unfamiliar electrical application, identifying the source of current, which effect it produces, and which specific property of that effect (e.g. controllable poles, strength variables, resistance-to-heat conversion) makes the application work.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe what happens to a compass needle near a current-carrying wire when the circuit is opened and closed, and can construct a basic electromagnet and demonstrate that its magnetic effect is present only when current flows.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works through simple circuits to produce magnetic and heating effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A student places a magnetic compass directly beneath a wire connected in a simple circuit. When the switch is closed, the compass needle deflects. When the switch is opened, the needle returns to its original position. Which statement best explains these observations?

options.label: A
options.text: A current-carrying wire produces a magnetic field around it, which disappears when the current stops flowing.

options.label: B
options.text: The battery produces a permanent magnetic field around all nearby objects, which disappears only when the battery is removed.

options.label: C
options.text: The compass needle is attracted to the copper in the wire regardless of whether current flows.

options.label: D
options.text: The switch itself acts as a magnet and deflects the needle when it is closed.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Misconception that the battery is the source of the magnetic field rather than the current in the wire, and that the field is permanent rather than current-dependent.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Confusion between electrical conductivity (copper carries current) and magnetic attraction — the student attributes the effect to the wire's material rather than the current flowing through it.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confusion between the mechanical function of the switch (completing the circuit) and the magnetic source — the student locates the magnetic effect at the switch rather than at the current-carrying wire.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggled with the compass activity can still demonstrate this outcome by reasoning from the pattern 'switch closed → needle moves, switch open → needle still', which directly maps to current-on → field present. Students who find the language of 'magnetic field' abstract can be asked to describe what the wire does to the space around it when current flows.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe what happens to a compass needle near a current-carrying wire when the circuit is opened and closed, and can construct a basic electromagnet and demonstrate that its magnetic effect is present only when current flows.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works through simple circuits to produce magnetic and heating effects.

assessment_items.question_text: An iron nail is wrapped with insulated wire and connected to a cell through a switch. Iron paper clips cling to the nail when the switch is closed but fall off when the switch is opened. Which conclusion is best supported by this observation?

options.label: A
options.text: Insulated wire prevents any magnetic effect, so the clips must be attracted by the iron nail itself.

options.label: B
options.text: The cell directly magnetises the nail through the wire, and opening the switch breaks the physical contact needed to hold the clips.

options.label: C
options.text: The coil carrying current creates a magnetic effect that exists only while current flows, making the nail attract the clips temporarily.

options.label: D
options.text: The iron nail permanently becomes a magnet after the first time current flows through the coil.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Misconception that brief current flow permanently magnetises the iron nail — confusing a temporary electromagnet with a permanent magnet, a key alternative conception flagged in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Confusion about the role of insulation — the student incorrectly infers that insulated wire blocks all effects, not understanding that insulation prevents short circuits while still allowing current to flow through the coil.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Misconception that the cell directly magnetises the nail and that opening the switch is a mechanical disconnection of a physical hold, rather than understanding that the magnetic field collapses when current stops.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can demonstrate the same understanding by describing the sequence of events (clips cling → switch open → clips fall) and linking each step to current state. Students who need a language scaffold can be asked to complete sentence frames: 'When current flows, the nail … because … When current stops, the nail … because …'

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the poles of an electromagnet, classify how varying current and coil turns affects its strength, and explain that reversing current direction reverses the poles.

competency.competency_text: Investigating properties of natural and artificial magnets and Earth as a magnet.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Variable changed | Number of paper clips lifted (Trial 1) | Number of paper clips lifted (Trial 2) | Number of paper clips lifted (Trial 3)
2 turns, 1 cell | 3 | 3 | 4
4 turns, 1 cell | 6 | 7 | 6
6 turns, 1 cell | 10 | 9 | 10
6 turns, 2 cells | 14 | 15 | 14
assessment_items.question_text: A student investigates what affects the strength of an electromagnet. Refer to the table provided. Which variable, when increased from 2 to 6 turns with one cell, shows the clearest pattern, and what does this pattern indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: Neither variable shows a clear pattern because the trial-to-trial variation makes the results unreliable.

options.label: B
options.text: The number of cells; increasing cells from 1 to 2 with 6 turns more than doubles the lifting power, showing current magnitude is the only factor.

options.label: C
options.text: The number of coil turns; increasing turns from 2 to 6 decreases lifting power because more wire adds resistance and weakens the magnet.

options.label: D
options.text: The number of coil turns; increasing turns from 2 to 6 with one cell triples the lifting power, indicating that more turns increases electromagnet strength.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confusion between the two variables — student correctly identifies that cells affect strength but incorrectly attributes the turns-only data rows to cell variation, or concludes that current magnitude is the sole factor without reading the turns data.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misconception that more wire means more resistance and therefore a weaker magnet, conflating the heating-effect concept of resistance with the turns-strength relationship in electromagnets.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Over-attention to trial-to-trial variation without understanding that small natural variation does not negate a clear directional trend — a reasoning error about data interpretation.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with reading multi-row tables can be directed to compare only the first and third rows (2 turns vs 6 turns, same 1-cell condition) to isolate the turns variable. Students who reason qualitatively rather than numerically can state the trend in words ('more turns → more clips') without computing a ratio.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the poles of an electromagnet, classify how varying current and coil turns affects its strength, and explain that reversing current direction reverses the poles.

competency.competency_text: Investigating properties of natural and artificial magnets and Earth as a magnet.

assessment_items.question_text: A student identifies the North pole of an electromagnet using a compass. She then swaps the two connecting wires at the battery terminals and tests the same end of the electromagnet with the compass again. What will she observe, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: The electromagnet will lose its poles entirely, because reversing the connections cancels out the magnetic field.

options.label: B
options.text: The same end will now be the South pole, because reversing current direction reverses the magnetic poles of the electromagnet.

options.label: C
options.text: The same end will now be the South pole, but only temporarily — the poles will return to their original positions once the current stabilises.

options.label: D
options.text: The same end will still be the North pole, because the number of turns and the iron core have not changed.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Misconception that pole identity is fixed by physical structure (turns, core) rather than by current direction — conflating the permanent properties of a bar magnet with the controllable properties of an electromagnet.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Misconception that reversing connections produces cancellation rather than reversal — possibly confusing current reversal with two opposing currents interfering with each other.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Correct identification of pole reversal but incorrect addition of a 'settling' or transient behaviour that has no basis in the chapter — a plausible-sounding distractor targeting students who over-generalise from AC or transient-current contexts.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who need a concrete scaffold can be asked to trace the direction of current through the coil before and after swapping, using an arrow on a diagram, to see that the winding direction relative to current flow determines the pole — the swap changes which end the current enters first.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the poles of an electromagnet, classify how varying current and coil turns affects its strength, and explain that reversing current direction reverses the poles.

competency.competency_text: Investigating properties of natural and artificial magnets and Earth as a magnet.

assessment_items.question_text: A cylindrical coil is wound on a paper tube, connected to a battery, and a compass is placed at each end. When an iron nail is inserted into the tube, a student claims 'the poles of the electromagnet changed.' Is the student correct? State whether the claim is correct or incorrect, identify what actually changes when the iron nail is inserted, and explain why inserting the iron nail does not change the pole identity.
expected_elements: States clearly that the student's claim is incorrect — inserting the iron nail does not change the poles.
Identifies what actually changes: the strength (number of clips lifted or magnetic force) increases when the iron nail is inserted.
Explains why pole identity is unchanged: the poles are determined by the direction of current through the coil, which has not changed, so the same end remains North and the same end remains South.
Distinguishes the two separable variables: pole identity (set by current direction) and magnetic strength (set by current magnitude, turns, and core material).

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find the written explanation difficult can be asked to draw two diagrams — coil without nail and coil with nail — labelling the N and S poles and the number of clips in each case, and then write one sentence stating what changed and what did not. This allows demonstration of the same conceptual distinction through a diagrammatic route.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and explain the heating effect of current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain that resistance in a conductor converts electrical energy to heat and can categorise examples of the heating effect as intentional (appliances) or unintended (energy loss, damage), with a one-sentence justification for each.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works through simple circuits to produce magnetic and heating effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A nichrome wire connected in a circuit becomes warm when one cell is used and becomes noticeably hotter when two cells are used. Which explanation best accounts for this observation?

options.label: A
options.text: Nichrome wire is specially designed to become magnetic when current flows, and it is this magnetism that produces heat.

options.label: B
options.text: The nichrome wire stores electrical energy inside it, and using more cells fills it up faster, releasing more heat.

options.label: C
options.text: The second cell adds extra heat of its own to the circuit, so the wire gets hotter when two cells are connected.

options.label: D
options.text: The wire resists the flow of current, and this resistance converts electrical energy into heat; more current from two cells produces more heat.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Misconception that wires store energy like a container — confusing the concept of current flow with charge accumulation, or conflating the wire with a capacitor or battery.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Cross-chapter confusion — student applies the magnetic effect of current (covered in Stage 1–2) to explain the heating effect, conflating the two distinct effects rather than identifying resistance as the heating mechanism.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misconception that the second cell adds its own thermal energy directly to the circuit, rather than increasing the current that then interacts with the wire's resistance to produce more heat.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggled with the abstract concept of resistance can demonstrate understanding by describing the observed pattern (more cells → wire hotter) and linking it to the idea that the wire opposes the flow and releases that energy as warmth. A sentence-completion scaffold — 'The wire gets hotter because it … and more current means …' — supports diverse expression.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and explain the heating effect of current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain that resistance in a conductor converts electrical energy to heat and can categorise examples of the heating effect as intentional (appliances) or unintended (energy loss, damage), with a one-sentence justification for each.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works through simple circuits to produce magnetic and heating effects.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Device or Situation | Purpose of heating
Electric room heater | Warm the room using hot coils
Electric kettle | Heat water for drinking
Long-distance power transmission cables | No intended purpose
Plastic insulation around wires in a device | No intended purpose
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. Which row correctly identifies a situation where the heating effect of current is unintended and potentially harmful, and which correctly identifies an intended use?

options.label: A
options.text: All four rows show intended heating because every wire in any device is chosen for its heating property.

options.label: B
options.text: Both the electric room heater and the electric kettle show unintended heating, because heating water or air is not the direct purpose of electricity.

options.label: C
options.text: Long-distance transmission cables and plastic insulation rows show unintended and potentially harmful heating; the heater and kettle rows show intended heating.

options.label: D
options.text: Long-distance transmission cables show an intended use; the electric room heater shows an unintended effect.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Reversal error — the student has swapped the categories, possibly because transmission cables involve large-scale electrical infrastructure and seem more 'electrical' than a heater, leading to mis-categorisation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Misconception that the heating effect is always unintended because electricity's 'real' purpose is light or motion — the student does not recognise that appliance designers deliberately exploit resistance heating.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Overgeneralisation — the student applies the true fact that all wires heat up to the false conclusion that all heating is intentional, failing to distinguish design intent from unavoidable physical effect.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the table approach challenging can be asked to classify each row using a simple question: 'Did the designer want this heat?' This reframes the task in terms of human intent rather than physics categorisation and allows the same distinction to be demonstrated with less technical language.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and explain the heating effect of current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain that resistance in a conductor converts electrical energy to heat and can categorise examples of the heating effect as intentional (appliances) or unintended (energy loss, damage), with a one-sentence justification for each.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works through simple circuits to produce magnetic and heating effects.

assessment_items.question_text: An electric iron heats up and smooths clothes when current flows through its heating element. At the same time, the outer plastic casing of the iron must not get hot. Using the concept of resistance and the heating effect of electric current, explain why the heating element gets hot while the plastic casing does not, and state one consequence that would occur if the casing were made of a material with high resistance instead of plastic.
expected_elements: States that the heating element is made of a material (such as nichrome) with high resistance, which converts electrical energy into heat when current flows through it.
States that the plastic casing does not carry current — it is an insulator — so no resistance-based heating occurs in it.
Identifies a specific consequence of using a high-resistance casing: it would heat up, creating a burn or fire hazard, or it would waste electrical energy as heat in an unwanted location.
Connects the consequence to the concept: heating occurs wherever current flows through a resistant material, so a resistant casing would experience the same heating effect as the element.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to articulate the mechanism in prose can draw a labelled diagram of the iron showing current path through the element and absence of current through the casing, then write one sentence per part. Students who know the outcome (casing would heat up) but cannot link it to resistance can be prompted: 'Which part does the current flow through, and what does that mean for where heat is produced?'

assessment_items.stage_label: Construct and explain sources of electric current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain how a chemical reaction between two different metals and an electrolyte produces electric current, and can compare Voltaic cells, dry cells, and rechargeable batteries across at least four attributes with justification.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works through simple circuits to produce magnetic and heating effects.

assessment_items.question_text: In a lemon cell constructed with a copper wire and an iron nail inserted into a lemon, a student notices the LED lights up. Her partner says 'the lemon itself is generating electricity.' Which response best corrects this claim?

options.label: A
options.text: The copper wire alone generates the electricity because copper is a good conductor; the lemon and iron nail are not needed.

options.label: B
options.text: The LED generates its own power when placed in the circuit; the lemon cell only completes the circuit but does not produce current.

options.label: C
options.text: The lemon juice acts as the electrolyte, and it is the chemical reaction between the two different metals (copper and iron) and the lemon juice that produces the electric current — not the lemon alone.

options.label: D
options.text: The partner is correct — lemons contain natural electricity in their juice that is released when the circuit is connected.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Misconception that the lemon's juice is inherently electrical — attributing the source of current to the liquid alone without recognising the necessity of two different metal electrodes and the chemical reaction between them.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Confusion between electrical conductivity (copper conducts) and electrochemical energy generation — the student attributes current production to the best conductor rather than to the electrode-electrolyte chemical interaction.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Fundamental reversal of the energy source — the student treats the LED as the power source and the lemon cell as merely a connector, possibly confusing the roles of source and load in a circuit.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who built the lemon cell can revisit their observation: if they used two copper wires instead of copper and iron, did the LED light? This experimental memory (or re-test) demonstrates that two different metals are necessary, making the abstract electrochemical principle concrete without additional explanation.

assessment_items.stage_label: Construct and explain sources of electric current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain how a chemical reaction between two different metals and an electrolyte produces electric current, and can compare Voltaic cells, dry cells, and rechargeable batteries across at least four attributes with justification.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works through simple circuits to produce magnetic and heating effects.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Attribute | Voltaic Cell | Dry Cell | Rechargeable Battery
Electrolyte form | Liquid (weak acid/salt solution) | Thick moist paste | Solid or gel
Portability | Low (liquid container needed) | High | High
Reusability | Single use | Single use | Multiple charge cycles
Disposal requirement | Liquid chemical waste | E-waste facility | E-waste facility
assessment_items.question_text: A field research team needs a portable power source for an instrument used in remote locations. The source must be reusable over many months, and safe disposal facilities are not available nearby. Refer to the table provided. Which cell or battery type is most suitable, and which attribute in the table is the most critical reason for your choice?

options.label: A
options.text: Dry cell; it is single-use and therefore the simplest technology, making it the safest choice when disposal facilities are unavailable.

options.label: B
options.text: Dry cell; the thick paste electrolyte makes it the most portable option, and portability is the most critical attribute for remote fieldwork.

options.label: C
options.text: Rechargeable battery; reusability over many charge cycles is the most critical attribute, since single-use cells would need frequent replacement and safe disposal — neither of which is possible remotely.

options.label: D
options.text: Voltaic cell; liquid electrolyte is best for remote use because it can be refreshed with any available liquid.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Misconception that the Voltaic cell's liquid electrolyte is an advantage in remote settings — confusing the need for a stable sealed electrolyte with the ability to top up a liquid supply, and ignoring the low-portability attribute.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Partial reasoning — student correctly identifies portability as a relevant attribute but fails to weigh reusability, which is more critical when the remote location makes resupply difficult; the student stops at the first relevant attribute rather than integrating multiple attributes.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Faulty logic — the student correctly identifies disposal as a concern but draws the opposite conclusion: choosing the single-use cell because it is 'simpler' rather than recognising that single-use cells require more frequent disposal, compounding the problem rather than solving it.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find multi-attribute reasoning difficult can be guided to cross out the options eliminated by each constraint in turn (must be portable → eliminate Voltaic cell; must be reusable → eliminate dry cell) rather than evaluating all attributes simultaneously. This stepwise elimination uses the same table data to reach the same conclusion.

assessment_items.stage_label: Construct and explain sources of electric current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain how a chemical reaction between two different metals and an electrolyte produces electric current, and can compare Voltaic cells, dry cells, and rechargeable batteries across at least four attributes with justification.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works through simple circuits to produce magnetic and heating effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A dry cell and a Voltaic cell both use two different conducting materials in contact with an electrolyte to produce electric current. A student claims 'they are basically the same thing — the only difference is that the dry cell uses a paste instead of a liquid.' Evaluate this claim. State two ways in which the student is correct and one important way in which the student's claim is incomplete or misleading, referring specifically to an attribute other than the electrolyte form.
expected_elements: Correctly states that both cells involve two different conducting materials (electrodes) and an electrolyte, and that in both a chemical reaction produces electric current — supporting the student's claim of similarity in principle.
Correctly states that the student is right about the electrolyte difference: Voltaic cell uses liquid; dry cell uses paste, making the dry cell more portable.

Identifies a significant attribute the student omits: the Voltaic cell uses rods of different metals partially immersed in a container (low portability, liquid spill risk), while the dry cell uses a zinc container as the negative terminal — the structure is fundamentally different, not just the electrolyte state.

Alternatively accepts: the student's claim is incomplete because it ignores disposal — both are single-use, but the dry cell's paste electrolyte may contain acids and toxic metals requiring e-waste disposal, which the claim does not address.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the evaluative framing can be asked to first list three attributes where the cells are the same and three where they differ, using the comparison table from the unit — then identify which difference the student's claim misses. This converts a critical evaluation task into a structured comparison task that demonstrates the same analytical outcome.

assessment_items.stage_label: Reason across effects and sources: electromagnets, heating, and cells in integrated application
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct a complete chain-of-reasoning explanation for an unfamiliar electrical application, identifying the source of current, which effect it produces, and which specific property of that effect (e.g. controllable poles, strength variables, resistance-to-heat conversion) makes the application work.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works through simple circuits to produce magnetic and heating effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A factory uses a crane-mounted lifting electromagnet to sort steel scrap from non-metallic waste on a conveyor belt. The crane operator switches the current on to pick up steel objects and switches it off over a collection bin to release them. Which chain of reasoning correctly explains why this system works, and why a permanent magnet could not perform the same task as effectively?

options.label: A
options.text: The electromagnet works because current through the coil produces a magnetic field that attracts steel; switching the current off collapses the field and releases the objects — a permanent magnet cannot be switched off, so it could not release objects on demand.

options.label: B
options.text: The electromagnet works because steel is attracted to any strong magnet; a permanent magnet could do the same job but would be heavier and harder to move.

options.label: C
options.text: The electromagnet works because the iron core becomes permanently magnetised each time current flows, and the operator demagnetises it by reversing the current; a permanent magnet lacks reversible polarity.

options.label: D
options.text: The electromagnet works using the heating effect of current — the coil heats up and this heat energy is what attracts the steel objects; a permanent magnet produces no heat and therefore no attraction.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Partial reasoning — student correctly identifies magnetic attraction but fails to identify the on-off controllability as the critical distinguishing property of the electromagnet, and incorrectly attributes the permanent magnet's limitation to weight rather than its inability to release objects.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misconception from Stage 2: the student confuses the reversibility of poles (reversing current reverses poles) with the on-off behaviour of the electromagnet — incorrectly claiming the iron core is permanently magnetised and then demagnetised each cycle, missing the key temporary nature of the electromagnet.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Cross-effect confusion — student applies the heating effect concept (also from this chapter) to the magnetic application scenario, attributing steel attraction to thermal energy rather than to the magnetic field produced by the current-carrying coil.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who need support can be asked to trace the chain in three steps before evaluating the options: (1) what does the current do in the coil? (2) what happens to the magnetic field when current stops? (3) why does that matter for the sorting job? This step-by-step trace supports the same integrated reasoning through a scaffolded pathway.

assessment_items.stage_label: Reason across effects and sources: electromagnets, heating, and cells in integrated application
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct a complete chain-of-reasoning explanation for an unfamiliar electrical application, identifying the source of current, which effect it produces, and which specific property of that effect (e.g. controllable poles, strength variables, resistance-to-heat conversion) makes the application work.

assessment_items.question_text: An engineer is designing a portable hair dryer that must be both light and capable of producing steady heat. She considers three power sources: a Voltaic cell with liquid electrolyte, a single-use dry cell, and a rechargeable lithium-ion battery. She also considers two heating elements: a short thick wire with low resistance and a long thin wire with high resistance. Which combination of power source and heating element is most appropriate for this application, and what is the most important reason?

options.label: A
options.text: Rechargeable lithium-ion battery and the long thin high-resistance wire, because the battery is portable and reusable, and the high-resistance wire converts more electrical energy to heat, which is the intended effect.

options.label: B
options.text: Rechargeable lithium-ion battery and the short thick low-resistance wire, because a rechargeable battery reduces waste and a low-resistance wire allows maximum current flow, which heats the dryer fastest.

options.label: C
options.text: Single-use dry cell and the long thin high-resistance wire, because the dry cell is simpler and the high-resistance wire produces heat — portability and reusability are secondary concerns for a hair dryer.

options.label: D
options.text: Voltaic cell with liquid electrolyte and the short thick wire, because liquid electrolytes provide the highest current and thick wires are safest.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Misconception about Voltaic cells — student over-generalises 'liquid provides more current' from the lemon-cell activity without reading the portability attribute from the comparison table; also confuses wire thickness with safety rather than with resistance and heating.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Failure to integrate the portability and reusability dimension — student correctly identifies the high-resistance wire but selects the single-use dry cell, ignoring that frequent replacement of single-use cells in a portable device is impractical, showing incomplete multi-attribute reasoning.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Correct source selection but incorrect element selection — student reasons correctly about the battery but then inverts the resistance-to-heat relationship, concluding that low resistance heats more (possibly confusing high current with high heat production from a low-resistance element, without noting that the element's own resistance is what produces the heat).

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find multi-variable design problems difficult can be guided to evaluate the two dimensions separately: first choose the best power source using the comparison table, then choose the best element using the resistance-to-heat relationship from Stage 3 — and finally combine the two justified choices. This separation reduces working-memory load while preserving the integration requirement.

assessment_items.stage_label: Reason across effects and sources: electromagnets, heating, and cells in integrated application
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct a complete chain-of-reasoning explanation for an unfamiliar electrical application, identifying the source of current, which effect it produces, and which specific property of that effect (e.g. controllable poles, strength variables, resistance-to-heat conversion) makes the application work.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works through simple circuits to produce magnetic and heating effects.

assessment_items.question_text: An electric bell uses an electromagnet to repeatedly strike a gong. When the circuit is closed, the electromagnet attracts an iron strip, which strikes the gong; this breaks the circuit momentarily, the electromagnet loses its magnetism, the strip springs back, the circuit closes again, and the cycle repeats. A student says: 'If we increased the number of turns in the electromagnet's coil, the bell would ring more loudly, but if we used a rechargeable battery instead of the dry cell, the bell would ring with a different note.' Evaluate both parts of the student's claim using concepts from the entire chapter — for each part, state whether you agree or disagree, and explain your reasoning using the relevant property of electromagnets or cells.
look_for: Correctly agrees with the first claim and provides the appropriate reasoning: more turns increases the strength of the electromagnet, so the iron strip is attracted more forcefully, striking the gong harder and producing a louder sound — drawing on the Stage 2 relationship between coil turns and magnetic strength.

Correctly disagrees with the second claim and provides the appropriate reasoning: the type of battery (dry cell vs rechargeable) determines portability and reusability, but both supply direct current at comparable voltage; the note (frequency and pitch) of the bell is determined by the mechanical properties of the gong and strip, not by the battery chemistry — the student has confused the energy source with the acoustic output.

Integrates evidence from across the chapter: uses the electromagnet-strength variable (Stage 2) for the first evaluation and the battery-comparison knowledge (Stage 4) for the second, demonstrating that these are independent systems within the same device.

Provides a counterfactual or correction for the second claim: correctly states what a change in battery type would and would not affect (e.g. it might affect how long the bell rings before the battery is exhausted, but not the note it produces).
Uses precise language from the chapter throughout: magnetic strength, number of turns, current, electrolyte, reusability — avoiding vague terms such as 'power' or 'electricity level'.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find the dual-claim structure cognitively demanding can be asked to address each claim in a separate paragraph, beginning each with 'I agree/disagree because…' and citing one specific piece of chapter evidence. This separates the two evaluations without reducing the depth required for either, allowing students who reason strongly on one part to demonstrate that strength clearly even if the second is less developed.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct a complete chain-of-reasoning explanation for an unfamiliar electrical application, identifying the source of current, which effect it produces, and which specific property of that effect (e.g. controllable poles, strength variables, resistance-to-heat conversion) makes the application work.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works through simple circuits to produce magnetic and heating effects.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Scenario | Power source available | Primary electrical effect needed | Specific property required | Suitable? (Yes/No) | Justification
A hospital MRI scanner must attract and release metal objects on demand | Mains electricity (treated as large rechargeable supply) | | | |
A remote weather station needs a heating coil to prevent instrument freezing; batteries must last many months without replacement | Rechargeable battery pack | | | |
A scrap yard wants to sort aluminium cans from steel cans using a magnet on a crane | Mains electricity | | | |
A student wants to build a simple cell using materials at home to power a small LED | Lemon, copper coin, iron nail | | |
assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. For each scenario: (1) identify which primary electrical effect (magnetic or heating) is needed; (2) state the specific property of that effect that makes it work in this scenario (e.g. on-off controllability, strength increase with turns, resistance-to-heat conversion); (3) decide whether the available power source is suitable for the scenario and record Yes or No; (4) write a justification of no more than two sentences explaining your suitability decision using one attribute of the power source from the chapter.
assessment_items.scaffold: For each row, ask yourself: Does this scenario need a magnetic effect or a heating effect? Which specific property of that effect (controllability, strength, resistance-to-heat) is essential here? Does the available power source match what the scenario demands in terms of reusability, portability, or chemical energy production? Use your answers to complete the table and write your justifications.
format_of_output: Completed table with all four rows filled in across all five columns
One justification sentence per scenario (may be written beneath each row or in a separate justification column)

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The Final Stage implied LO requires students to reason across both effects and across multiple source types simultaneously for unfamiliar applications; a classification-with-justification table is the most direct demonstration vehicle because it forces explicit identification of effect, property, and source suitability for each scenario rather than allowing students to address only the most familiar case.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can integrate magnetic effect knowledge (on-off control, strength variables), heating effect knowledge (resistance-to-heat mechanism), and battery/cell knowledge (reusability, portability, chemical energy source) across four distinct unfamiliar scenarios — the core cognitive operation of the Final Stage.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold is structured so that each row isolates one scenario, and the four-column structure separates the four reasoning steps (effect identification, property identification, suitability judgement, justification). A teacher reading student responses should check whether the effect identification and property identification are consistent with each other — a student who writes 'magnetic effect' but then names resistance-to-heat as the property has made a cross-effect error that the column structure will reveal.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: correctly identify the effect for all four scenarios (magnetic for MRI and scrap yard, heating for weather station, chemical-to-electrical for lemon cell); name a specific property for each (e.g. 'on-off controllability' for MRI, 'resistance-to-heat conversion' for weather station); provide justified suitability decisions that cite a specific power-source attribute from the chapter (e.g. 'rechargeable battery is suitable because it is reusable over many charge cycles without replacement'). Weak responses: conflate the two effects; state suitability without citing a source attribute; or repeat the same property for all scenarios regardless of context. Note for the scrap-yard row: aluminium is not attracted to a magnet — a strong response will identify that the scenario as stated will not work for aluminium sorting and explain why, demonstrating evaluative reasoning beyond classification.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the full table daunting can complete two rows of their choice, ensuring one magnetic-effect scenario and one heating-effect scenario are included — this preserves the cross-effect integration requirement while reducing volume. Students who prefer to reason verbally can write their chain of reasoning for each scenario in prose beneath the table and leave the cells as single-word answers, with the prose carrying the justification requirement.
